en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
First Part
2.2 Section on the Occurrence of Offenses 1.
Chapter on Defeat (Pārājika) How many offenses does a lustful bhikkhunī commit when she consents to physical contact from a lustful man?
A lustful bhikkhunī, consenting to physical contact with a lustful man, incurs three offenses:
if she consents to being grasped below the collarbone and above the kneecaps, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika);
if she consents to being grasped above the collarbone and below the kneecaps, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If she consents to being touched on the body by one who is attached, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
When a lustful bhikkhunī consents to bodily contact with a lustful man, she incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does a bhikkhunī who conceals an offense incur when she conceals an offense?
A nun who conceals an offense incurs three offenses while concealing it:
if she conceals an offense entailing expulsion knowing it to be such, she incurs an offense entailing expulsion;
if she conceals it while being in doubt, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If she conceals a failure in conduct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus, a nun who conceals a fault incurs these three offenses while concealing that fault.
How many offenses does a nun who sides with one who has been suspended incur if she does not desist even after being admonished up to the third time?
A nun who sides with one who has been suspended and does not desist even after being formally admonished up to three times incurs three offenses:
on the motion, a dukkaṭa;
on the two subsequent proclamations, thullaccayas.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
A nun who follows one who has been suspended and does not desist after being admonished up to three times incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does she incur while fulfilling the eighth ground?
While fulfilling the eighth offense, one incurs three offenses:
when she goes because she has been told by a man, “Come to such-and-such a place,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
at the mere moment she enters the reach of the man’s hand, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she fulfills the eighth basis, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
While fulfilling the eighth basis, she incurs these three offenses.
The section on defeats (pārājika) is concluded.
2. Saṅghādisesa Section:
A nun who brings a groundless accusation while making a legal claim incurs three offenses.
When she reports it to one person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she informs a second person, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
at the conclusion of half [the instruction], there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
One who ordains a female thief incurs three offenses.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for the motion;
there are offenses of serious transgression for two proclamations;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
A nun traveling from one village to another incurs three offenses:
as she goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when she steps across the boundary for the first time, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If she steps across the second foot, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

If she reinstates a nun who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—without having obtained the permission of the Saṅgha that performed the act and without knowing the consent of the group—she incurs three offenses: for the motion (ñatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and so on for the proclamation and the completion].
With two proclamations, there are *thullaccaya* offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
A lustful nun who, with her own hand, accepts fresh or cooked food from the hand of a lustful man and eats it, incurs three offenses.
If he accepts [the food] thinking, “I will eat it, I will consume it,” there is a thullaccaya offense;
for every mouthful swallowed, there is a saṅghādisesa offense;
if he accepts water or a tooth-stick, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“Noble lady, what can this man do to you, whether he is lustful or not,
since you are free from lust? Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this man gives you,
eat it or consume it”— by thus inciting her, she incurs three offenses.
If, at her word, one accepts [the food] thinking, "I shall eat it, I shall consume it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
at the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A bhikkhunī who, being angry, does not desist after being exhorted up to the third time, incurs three offenses:
on the motion, a dukkaṭa;
with the two proclamations, thullaccayas.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā), there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

A nun who has been rebuked in regard to some legal issue (adhikaraṇa) and does not desist after being pressed up to three times incurs three offenses: for the motion (ñatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and so on for the subsequent proclamations].
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
Bhikkhunīs who are in association and do not desist even after being admonished up to three times incur three kinds of offenses.
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
“Venerable ladies, you should live in association; do not live apart. If she does not desist even after being exhorted up to three times, she incurs three offenses:
a *dukkaṭa* for the formal motion (*ñatti*), and two *thullaccaya*s for the two subsequent proclamations (*kammavācā*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
The *saṅghādisesa* offenses are finished.
3. The Section on Forfeiture (*Nissaggiyakaṇḍa*).
One who makes a hoard of cloth incurs one offense:
an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
One who, having determined an out-of-season robe to be an in-season robe, distributes it, incurs two offenses.
In the act of causing it to be distributed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been distributed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
By exchanging a robe with a nun and then taking it back, she incurs two offenses.
In the act of taking it away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been taken away, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If she requests one thing and then requests another, she incurs two offenses.
If she requests it, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of requesting;
when it has been requested, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, having asked for one thing, she asks for something else, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be exchanged, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
By exchanging one thing for another with a requisite belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for a different purpose, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be exchanged, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of proposing;
once it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).

If she causes something else to be exchanged for a requisite belonging to the Saṅgha that was intended for another purpose, designated for another, and obtained through formal request, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be exchanged, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
when it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If she causes something else to be exchanged by means of a requisite intended for another purpose, designated for another, and belonging to the community, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be exchanged, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
once it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

If she causes something else to be exchanged for a requisite that was intended for another purpose, designated for another, belonging to the community, or obtained by request, she incurs two offenses.
When she causes it to be bartered for, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
when it has been bartered for, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
When she causes something else to be bartered for using a requisite intended for another purpose, dedicated to another, and obtained by personal request, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be exchanged, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If she causes a heavy cloak worth more than four *karṣas* to be exchanged, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be bartered for, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of procurement;
when it has been bartered for, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If she causes a light cloak to be bartered for, exceeding two and a half *kaṃsa* [in weight], she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be bartered, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once it has been bartered, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
The offenses entailing relinquishment and confession are finished.
4. Pācittiyakaṇḍa 4.1.
Lasuṇavagga:
One incurs two offenses when eating garlic.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If she has hair removed from the private parts, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes it to be gathered, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
when it has been gathered, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who strikes with the palm of the hand incurs two offenses.
While making it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when it is made, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who takes up a dildo incurs two offenses.
When she takes it up, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort;
when it has been taken up, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If she takes up water-washing [of the feet] with more than two finger-joints [of soap-residue], she incurs two offenses.
When she takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
when it has been taken, there is an offense entailing expiation.
While a bhikkhu is eating, she commits two offenses by standing over him with drinking water or a fan.
If she stands within arm’s reach, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
if she stands having left arm’s reach, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By requesting raw grain and eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts [food] thinking, “I will eat,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful she swallows, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she discards excrement, urine, refuse, or food scraps over a wall or over a fence, she incurs two offenses.
If she discards it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the act;
once discarded, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If she discards feces, urine, refuse, or food scraps on green vegetation, she incurs two offenses.
If she discards it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
once discarded, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
For going to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music, she incurs two offenses.
If she goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
wherever she stands and sees or hears [the sound], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The first section on garlic is concluded.
4.2. The Chapter on Darkness at Night.
In the dark of night, without a lamp, if she stands alone with a man, she incurs two offenses.
If she stands within arm’s reach, she incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she stands having left the reach of hand, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Standing alone with a man in a concealed place, she incurs two offenses:
while standing within the reach of hand, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya); [if she leaves the reach of hand, it is an offense of wrong-doing].
If she stands having left the reach of hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Standing alone with a man in the open air, she incurs two offenses:
while standing within the reach of hand, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); [if she stands beyond the reach of hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing].
If she stands having left the reach of the hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she stands one-on-one with a man on a carriage road, in a street, or at a crossroads, she incurs two offenses:
while she stands within the reach of the hand, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); [if she leaves the reach of the hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing].
If she stands having left the reach of hand-contact, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, if she departs without asking permission from the owners, she incurs two offenses:
when she steps across the threshold of the sheltered area with her first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she steps across the second foot, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having approached families after the meal, if she sits down on a seat without asking permission from the owners, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of sitting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the completion of the act, an offense of expiation].
If she sits down, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having approached families at an improper time and, without having asked the owners for permission, if she spreads out a bed or has one spread out and then sits down upon it, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of sitting down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the act of sitting down itself, there is an offense of expiation].
If she sits down [in such a manner], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
By censuring another on account of what was wrongly grasped or wrongly understood, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of censuring, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If she reviles [him], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she curses herself or another with reference to hell or the holy life, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of cursing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If she curses him, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If, weeping, she strikes herself repeatedly, she incurs two offenses:
for striking her and for weeping, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If she laughs or cries, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The second section, on the dark of night, is concluded.
4.3. The Section on Bathing.
A naked woman bathing commits two offenses:
for the act of bathing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
at the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a water-bathing robe made that exceeds the proper measure incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a bhikkhunī, having had a robe unsewn or having had it unsewn, neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, she incurs one offense:
a pācittiya.
If she lets the five-day period for the distribution of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) pass by, she incurs one offense.
It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who wears a robe intended for exchange incurs two offenses:
for the act of wearing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for the completion of the act, an offense of expiation].
If she wears it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
By creating an obstacle to the community’s acquisition of robes, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of doing so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If she does so, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

One who obstructs a lawful distribution of robes incurs two offenses: for the act of obstructing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the obstruction itself, an offense of expiation].
If she is refused, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
When giving a robe of an ascetic (samaṇacīvara) to a householder, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of giving, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and upon completion, an offense of expiation].
If it is given, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For one who lets the robe-season pass while still having an expectation of a weak robe-material, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of letting it pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and when it has passed, an offense of expiation].
If it has passed [the time], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who obstructs a legitimate suspension of the kaṭhina incurs two offenses:
for the act of obstructing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If she is warded off, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The third section on bathing is concluded.
4.4. The Section on Pressing Upwards (tuvaṭṭa).
Two bhikkhunīs who lie down on the same bed incur two offenses:
for the act of lying down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once they have lain down, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Two bhikkhunīs, lying down together on the same sheet and the same coverlet, incur two offenses:
for the act of lying down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once they have lain down, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
A bhikkhunī who intentionally causes discomfort incurs two offenses:
for the act of doing so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when it is completed, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If she neither attends to a co-resident nun who is suffering nor makes an effort to have her attended to, she incurs one offense:
a pācittiya.
If, having given a dwelling place to a bhikkhunī, she becomes angry and displeased and then ejects her, she incurs two offenses.
In the act of ejecting her, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once she has been ejected, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
A nun who is overly familiar with laypeople and does not desist after being admonished up to three times incurs two offenses.
By the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
at the conclusion of the formal act, there is an offense of expiation.
When traveling on a journey without a caravan through a region within the kingdom that is considered dangerous and fearful, she incurs two offenses.
If she sets out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort;
when she has set out, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
When traveling on foot without a caravan through a foreign country considered dangerous and fearful, she incurs two offenses.
If she sets out, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the preparation;
when she has set out, there is an offense entailing expiation.
While wandering on tour during the rainy season, she incurs two offenses.
If she sets out, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of setting out;
when she has set out, there is an offense entailing expiation.
A nun who has completed the rains residence commits one offense if she does not set out on a journey.
An offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fourth chapter: The Chapter on Rubbing.
4.5. The Chapter on Picture Galleries.
When going to see a royal palace, a pleasure house, a park, a garden, or a lotus pond, she incurs two offenses:
as she goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
where she stands and sees it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While using a high seat or a luxurious couch, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of using it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been used, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While spinning thread, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of spinning, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every winding and unwinding, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While performing services for a householder, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of doing so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once it is done, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
When a bhikkhunī is addressed, “Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,” and having agreed by saying “Very well,” she neither settles it nor makes an effort to settle it, she incurs one offense:
a pācittiya.
When giving fresh or cooked food with her own hand to a householder, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, she incurs two offenses.
When she makes the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
when it has been given, there is an offense entailing expiation.
By using a lodging-cloth without having relinquished it, she incurs two offenses.
While consuming it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the preliminary action;
once it has been consumed, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who sets out on a journey without having relinquished her dwelling incurs two offenses.
If she steps across the enclosure with her first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if she steps across with her second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By learning a worldly craft (tiracchānavijjā), she incurs two offenses.
If she masters it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
for every word, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If she teaches secular lore (tiracchānavijjā), she incurs two offenses.
In the act of causing [it] to be recited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fifth section, on the picture-gallery.
4.6. Ārāmavagga:
Entering a monastery known to have monks without asking permission, one incurs two offenses.
When she crosses the boundary with her first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she steps beyond the second foot, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While abusing and reviling a bhikkhu, she incurs two offenses: for the act of abusing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If she reviles him, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, being fierce, she abuses the community, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of abusing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and an offense of expiation upon completion].
If she has been reviled, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she has been invited or dismissed from a meal, yet eats either hard food or soft food, she incurs two offenses:
if she accepts it with the thought, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [if she then eats it, there is an offense of expiation].
For every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who is stingy with respect to families incurs two offenses:
for the act of being stingy, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for each mouthful taken by the recipient, there is an offense of expiation].
If she is envious, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
While residing for the rains in a monastery where no monks are present, she incurs two offenses:
if, thinking “I shall spend the rains retreat,” she prepares a lodging, sets out drinking water and water for washing, and sweeps the courtyard, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
At the rising of the dawn, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
A nun who has completed the rains residence and does not perform the invitation ceremony before both Saṅghas in three respects incurs one offense:
an offense of expiation.
If she does not go for the sake of exhortation or for communal living, she commits one offense:
a *pācittiya*.
If she neither asks about the *uposatha* nor requests the exhortation, she commits one offense.
An offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she causes a boil or a wound arising in the private parts to be lanced by a man, one-on-one, without having informed the Saṅgha or a group, she commits two offenses:
for the act of causing it to be lanced, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for the completion of the act, an offense of expiation].
If it is broken, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The sixth section, on the Monastery (ārāmavagga), is concluded. 4.7.
The section on pregnant women (gabbhinīvagga).
One who ordains a pregnant woman incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who ordains a woman who is breastfeeding incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort;
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a nun ordains a trainee nun who has not trained for two years in the six rules, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one gives the full admission to a trainee nun who has trained for two years in the six rules but has not been authorized by the Saṅgha, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of giving the full admission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once she has been fully admitted, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who ordains a married woman who is less than twelve years old incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If she gives the full admission to a married girl who is twelve years old but has not trained for two years in the six rules, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of giving her the full admission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once she has been given the full admission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she gives the full admission to a married girl who is twelve years old, has trained for two years in the six rules, but has not been authorized by the Saṅgha, she incurs two offenses:
there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of undertaking;
once she has given the full admission, there is an offense entailing expiation.
Having ordained a co-resident nun, if for two years she neither assists her nor causes her to be assisted, she commits one offense:
a pācittiya.
If she does not follow the preceptor who has ordained her for two years, she commits one offense: a pācittiya.
An offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Having given full admission to a co-resident nun, if one neither dismisses her nor causes her to be dismissed, one incurs one offense:
an offense entailing expiation.
The Seventh Chapter on Pregnant Women.
4.8. The Chapter on Maidens:
One who ordains a maiden who is less than twenty years of age incurs two offenses.
If she causes [her] to go forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once she has caused her to go forth, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who causes a girl who is more than twenty years old, but who has not trained for two years in the six rules while living as a maiden, to go forth incurs two offenses.
If she causes [her] to go forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
once she has been caused to go forth, there is an offense of expiation.

She incurs two offenses by causing one who is a full twenty years of age, who has been a maiden for two years and has trained in the six rules, to go forth when she has not been authorized by the Saṅgha.
If she causes [a girl] to go forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once she has caused her to go forth, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who causes a girl less than twelve years old to go forth incurs two offenses.
If she causes [a girl] to go forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once she has caused her to go forth, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who causes a girl to go forth who is less than twelve years old and has not been authorized by the Saṅgha incurs two offenses.
If she causes her to be ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
once she has been ordained, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If, when told, “Enough, noble lady, with ordaining you for now,” she agrees by saying “Very well,” but later falls into a state of criticism, she incurs two offenses.
If she reviles [her], there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of reviling;
if she is reviled, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Having said to a trainee nun, “If you, noble lady, will give me a robe, I will ordain you,” and then neither ordaining her nor making an effort to have her ordained, she incurs one offense.
An offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Having said to a trainee nun, “If you, noble lady, will follow me for two years, I shall ordain you,” yet neither ordaining her nor making an effort to have her ordained, she incurs one offense:
a pācittiya.
One who ordains a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) who is closely associated with men, closely associated with boys, fierce, and a dwelling place of sorrow, incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who ordains a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) who has not been permitted by her mother and father or by her husband incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
By giving her consent while she is on probation, one who is ordaining a trainee incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once she has been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Ordaining [a girl] every year, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she ordains two [nuns] in one year, she incurs two offenses:
for the act of ordaining, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once they have been ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The eighth chapter: The Chapter on Maidens.
4.9. The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
One who wears an umbrella and footwear incurs two offenses.
While making the effort to carry it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been carried, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
While traveling by vehicle, one incurs two offenses.
In the act of riding, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once ridden, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who wears a hip-cord incurs two offenses.
While making the effort to wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is worn, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who wears female ornaments incurs two offenses.
While making the effort to wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is worn, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
She incurs two offenses while bathing with perfumes and ointments.
She bathes: there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
at the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who bathes with scented sesamum paste incurs two offenses.
When she bathes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of preparation;
at the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
When a bhikkhunī has herself rubbed or massaged, she incurs two offenses.
If she causes [a woman] to be massaged, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort;
once massaged, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
A female trainee (sikkhamānā) who causes [a woman] to be massaged or rubbed incurs two offenses.
If she causes herself to be massaged, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the effort;
once massaged, there is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).
A female novice who causes herself to be massaged and causes herself to be rubbed commits two offenses.
If she causes herself to be massaged, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once massaged, there is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who causes a female lay follower to massage her or rub her body commits two offenses.
If she causes herself to be massaged, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
once massaged, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If she sits on a seat in front of a bhikkhu without asking permission, she incurs two offenses.
As she sits down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once seated, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By asking a question of a monk who has not been granted leave, she incurs two offenses.
If she asks, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the attempt;
when asked, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Entering a village without wearing her upper robe (asaṅkaccikā), she incurs two offenses.
If he steps over the enclosure with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if he steps over with the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
This concludes the ninth section, the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
The Minor Section is finished.
5. The Chapter on Offenses Requiring Confession:
By requesting ghee and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting oil and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful she swallows, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting honey and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful she swallows, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting molasses and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful she swallows, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
Having requested fish, she incurs two offenses while eating.
If she accepts it with the intention, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting meat and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts [the food] thinking, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful she swallows, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting milk and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
By requesting curd and then eating it, she incurs two offenses.
If she accepts it thinking, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
The eight offenses entailing confession are finished.
The second section, on the completion of the offense, is finished.
